input.strategy_title: AMD GPU (ROCm) enablement for serving and training
input.strategy_markdown:
## Problem Statement

Two strategic customers are standardizing on AMD Instinct accelerators and need
RHOAI to serve and train on ROCm. Upstream vLLM and PyTorch both publish ROCm
support, but the platform ships only CUDA runtime builds, and we have no
first-hand data on functional or performance parity for our supported model
set. Feature and performance validation requires physical AMD GPU hardware —
none exists in our CI fleet today — and upstream ROCm image cadence is
controlled by AMD and the upstream communities.

## High-Level Requirements

| ID | Priority | Requirement |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| HLR-1 | P0 | A validation campaign on physical AMD Instinct hardware establishes functional and performance parity data for vLLM serving of the supported model set, producing the go/no-go scope for productization. |
| HLR-2 | P0 | A supported vLLM ROCm serving runtime is productized for the models the validation campaign clears. |
| HLR-3 | P1 | PyTorch training on ROCm is supported for single- and multi-GPU jobs admitted through Kueue, with amd.com/gpu quota handling. |
| HLR-4 | P2 | Documentation states supported AMD hardware, driver prerequisites, and the validated model list. |

## Affected Components

- KServe
- Serving Runtimes
- Training Operator
- Distributed Workloads

## Out of Scope

- Intel Gaudi or other non-AMD accelerator families
- AMD GPU sharing/partitioning support

## Open Questions

1. Hardware access: the validation campaign (HLR-1) needs dedicated AMD
   Instinct nodes — procurement or partner-lab access is unresolved.
2. Upstream ROCm build cadence: whether AMD's runtime image releases align
   with our release trains is outside our control.

# AMD Instinct ROCm validation campaign for vLLM serving parity

## Description

Resolve the functional and performance parity question for vLLM serving on AMD Instinct accelerators: run a validation campaign on physical AMD GPU hardware covering the supported model set, and produce the go/no-go report that determines the productization scope for a supported vLLM ROCm serving runtime. This epic resolves the strategy's central unknown — the platform ships only CUDA runtime builds and has no first-hand parity data for ROCm.

## Scope

- Stand up the validation environment on dedicated AMD Instinct nodes: ROCm driver stack and GPU device plugin exposing `amd.com/gpu` resources, with the environment configuration documented for reproducibility. (Hardware availability itself — procurement or partner-lab access — is an external precondition tracked as a risk, not a deliverable.)
- Run functional validation: serve each model in the supported model set with a vLLM ROCm runtime build, deployed end-to-end through KServe InferenceServices backed by a ServingRuntime.
- Run performance validation: measure serving throughput and latency for each model against the CUDA baseline builds, on comparable hardware where available.
- Produce the go/no-go report: per-model functional pass/fail, performance parity data, and a recommended productization scope (the cleared model list).

## Acceptance Criteria

- A validated report exists covering every model in the supported model set, with per-model functional pass/fail results and performance measurements against the CUDA baseline.
- Each validated model was exercised end-to-end as a KServe InferenceService backed by a vLLM ROCm serving runtime on AMD Instinct hardware.
- The report states a go/no-go recommendation with an explicit productization scope (cleared model list) derived from the measured data.
- The validation environment configuration (node setup, driver versions, device plugin) is documented sufficiently to reproduce the campaign.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1 (P0): validation campaign on physical AMD Instinct hardware establishing functional and performance parity data for vLLM serving of the supported model set, producing the go/no-go scope for productization.

## Risks

- Hardware access is unresolved: dedicated AMD Instinct nodes require procurement or partner-lab access controlled by parties outside this strategy. The campaign cannot start until access is granted; this is a schedule risk on this epic and everything downstream.
- Upstream ROCm runtime image cadence is controlled by AMD and the upstream communities; the campaign must pin whatever image release is current, and results are specific to that pin.

# Productize supported vLLM ROCm serving runtime

## Description

Productize a supported vLLM ROCm serving runtime for the model set cleared by the validation campaign's go/no-go report, shipped alongside the existing CUDA runtime builds. Today only CUDA (NVIDIA) builds are productized; ROCm builds exist upstream but are neither shipped nor supported.

## Scope

- Build and release a vLLM ROCm runtime image from the midstream vLLM repository, pinned to a released upstream ROCm base image, released per platform version through the existing build pipeline.
- Define the ServingRuntime/ClusterServingRuntime resources for the ROCm build, requesting `amd.com/gpu` resources, coexisting with the existing CUDA runtimes in the same cluster.
- Support exactly the model list cleared by the validation campaign's go/no-go report (the cleared list is an input to this epic, produced by the campaign).
- Validate the passive KServe surface: KServe InferenceServices deploy and serve predictions with the ROCm runtime under the existing KServe lifecycle (no KServe code changes).

## Acceptance Criteria

- The vLLM ROCm serving runtime is productized and released per platform version, built from the midstream vLLM repository with its build pipeline green.
- Every model on the campaign's cleared list serves successfully through a KServe InferenceService backed by the ROCm runtime on AMD Instinct hardware.
- The runtime image pins a released upstream ROCm base image, and the pin is recorded so it can be re-evaluated against each release train (upstream cadence is externally controlled).
- The ServingRuntime resources request `amd.com/gpu` and deploy alongside existing CUDA runtimes in the same cluster without interference.
- The supported model list for the ROCm runtime is stated and matches the campaign's cleared list.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-2 (P0): a supported vLLM ROCm serving runtime is productized for the models the validation campaign clears.

## Risks

- Upstream ROCm build cadence may not align with platform release trains; mitigation is the recorded image pin plus per-train re-evaluation, not a scope change.
- The cleared model list is not known until the validation campaign reports; this epic's scope is gated on that report (rewrite: scope shrinks to the cleared models, or descope entirely if no models clear).

# PyTorch ROCm training support in the Training Operator

## Description

Support PyTorch training on ROCm for single- and multi-GPU jobs run through the Training Operator: PyTorchJobs using PyTorch ROCm runtime images run to completion on AMD Instinct nodes, including multi-GPU and multi-node distributed topologies, with admission through Kueue when workload queueing is enabled.

## Scope

- Enable PyTorchJob workers to run on AMD Instinct nodes: PyTorch ROCm runtime images, `amd.com/gpu` resource requests, and any required node affinity or tolerations for AMD GPU nodes.
- Verify single-GPU and multi-GPU (including multi-node) PyTorchJob topologies work on ROCm with distributed training intact.
- Verify PyTorchJobs requesting `amd.com/gpu` are admitted through Kueue when workload queueing is enabled (end-to-end with the platform's queueing layer).

## Acceptance Criteria

- A single-GPU PyTorchJob using a PyTorch ROCm runtime image completes training successfully on AMD Instinct hardware.
- A multi-GPU PyTorchJob completes with distributed training intact (workers communicate across `amd.com/gpu` devices) on AMD Instinct hardware.
- A PyTorchJob requesting `amd.com/gpu` is admitted through Kueue queueing when workload queueing is enabled.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-3 (P1, partial — job/runtime side): PyTorch training on ROCm is supported for single- and multi-GPU jobs admitted through Kueue.

## Risks

- Validation requires access to AMD Instinct hardware (shared dependency with the rest of the strategy's hardware access risk).
- The verification ACs above run on AMD Instinct nodes whose stand-up (ROCm driver stack, `amd.com/gpu` device plugin) is in scope of the serving validation campaign, which runs in parallel with this epic. Training verification either shares that environment once it is stood up (coordinate scheduling with the campaign team) or procures its own AMD nodes; either way the node environment itself is not re-delivered here. This is a coordination point, not a blocking dependency — the training work is not gated on serving-parity results.
- PyTorch ROCm runtime image availability follows upstream PyTorch ROCm release cadence.

# Kueue amd.com/gpu quota handling for ROCm workloads

## Description

Kueue quota handling for AMD GPUs: ClusterQueue/LocalQueue configuration covering `amd.com/gpu` resources so that ROCm training workloads are admitted with correct quota accounting and all-or-nothing gang semantics, matching how NVIDIA GPU quota is handled today.

## Scope

- Define quota configuration (ClusterQueue/LocalQueue resource flavors) that covers `amd.com/gpu` resources on AMD Instinct node pools.
- Ensure quota accounting and admission — including all-or-nothing (waitForPodsReady) gang semantics — work correctly for workloads requesting `amd.com/gpu`.
- Cover both single-GPU and multi-GPU job topologies in quota and admission behavior.
- Verify end-to-end that accelerated jobs requesting `amd.com/gpu` (e.g. PyTorchJobs) are admitted and run on AMD Instinct nodes with quota enforced.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A ClusterQueue/LocalQueue configuration admits workloads requesting `amd.com/gpu` with correct quota accounting against the configured quotas.
- All-or-nothing (waitForPodsReady) admission semantics hold for multi-GPU jobs requesting `amd.com/gpu`: a job is admitted only when its full GPU allocation fits.
- End-to-end: an accelerated job requesting `amd.com/gpu` is admitted through a queue and runs to completion on AMD Instinct nodes with quota enforced.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-3 (P1, partial — quota/admission side): single- and multi-GPU jobs admitted through Kueue, with amd.com/gpu quota handling.

## Risks

- Validation requires access to AMD Instinct hardware (shared dependency with the rest of the strategy's hardware access risk).
- The end-to-end admission AC above runs on AMD Instinct nodes whose stand-up (ROCm driver stack, `amd.com/gpu` device plugin) is in scope of the serving validation campaign, which runs in parallel with this epic. Quota/admission verification either shares that environment once it is stood up (coordinate scheduling with the campaign team) or procures its own AMD nodes; either way the node environment itself is not re-delivered here. This is a coordination point, not a blocking dependency — the training work is not gated on serving-parity results.

# Document AMD GPU (ROCm) support

## Description

Author user-facing documentation for AMD GPU (ROCm) enablement: supported AMD hardware, driver prerequisites, and the validated model list, plus how to configure serving and training workloads on ROCm.

## Scope

Content outline (authored through the Red Hat docs content process):

- Supported AMD Instinct hardware: which accelerators are supported for serving and training.
- Driver and ROCm prerequisites for cluster administrators (node setup, device plugin, `amd.com/gpu` resource exposure).
- The validated model list for vLLM ROCm serving, as cleared by the validation campaign.
- How to configure vLLM ROCm serving through ServingRuntime/InferenceService resources.
- How to configure PyTorch training on ROCm: PyTorchJob submission and Kueue queue/quota configuration for `amd.com/gpu`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Published documentation states the supported AMD hardware, driver prerequisites, and the validated model list.
- Serving and training configuration topics cover the ROCm runtime and `amd.com/gpu` quota setup as delivered by the implementation work.
- The content is technically reviewed against the implemented behavior (reviewed by the owning engineers, not just editorially).

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-4 (P2): documentation states supported AMD hardware, driver prerequisites, and the validated model list.

## Notes

- The validated model list is an input produced by the validation campaign's go/no-go report; documentation cannot be finalized until serving productization and training support land.

## Dependency DAG

```mermaid
graph TD
    E001["E001 ROCm validation campaign"] --> E002["E002 vLLM ROCm runtime productization"]
    E002 --> E005["E005 Documentation"]
    E003["E003 PyTorchJob ROCm support"] --> E005

```

## DAG Justification

| Edge | Rule | Rationale |
|------|------|-----------|
| E001 → E002 | Rule 3 (Investigation edge) | The campaign's go/no-go report determines which models the productized runtime must support — a true gate (`rewrite`: productization scope shrinks or descope if models fail parity). Recorded as `gated_by` + `gate_failure_impact` on E002. |
| E002 → E005 | Rule 11 (docs-authoring last) | Documentation describes what was built; blocked by every Implementation epic. |
| E003 → E005 | Rule 11 (docs-authoring last) | Same. |
| E004 → E005 | Rule 11 (docs-authoring last) | Same. |

**Deliberate non-edges:**

- E002 ∥ E003 ∥ E004 (Rule 14): different components in different midstream repos (vllm, training-operator, kueue) with no shared build-against artifacts — all parallel.
- E003 ∥ E004: same team but different components/repos; Kueue quota configuration and PyTorchJob ROCm support are complementary surfaces verified together end-to-end (AC on both), not serialized.
- E001 ∥ E003/E004: the campaign gates serving productization (HLR-2) only. Training enablement (HLR-3, P1) delivers independent value and is not gated by serving parity results. Environment coordination (not a DAG edge): E003/E004 verification ACs run on AMD Instinct nodes whose stand-up (ROCm driver stack, `amd.com/gpu` device plugin) is in E001's scope — training verification either shares that environment once stood up or procures its own AMD nodes; recorded as Risks on both training epics.
- No `konflux-onboarding` epic: all components already exist in the platform and are Konflux-onboarded per architecture context; Rule 25 build-pipeline-green is an AC on E002, never an edge.

## HLR Traceability Matrix

| HLR | Priority | Epic(s) |
|-----|----------|---------|
| HLR-1 — validation campaign on physical AMD Instinct hardware producing go/no-go scope | P0 | E001 |
| HLR-2 — supported vLLM ROCm serving runtime productized for cleared models | P0 | E002 |
| HLR-3 — PyTorch training on ROCm via Kueue with amd.com/gpu quota | P1 | E003, E004 |
| HLR-4 — documentation of supported hardware, drivers, validated model list | P2 | E005 |

No HLR is bundled: each maps to epics along clean component boundaries. HLR-3 spans two epics because Training Operator and Distributed Workloads are distinct components in distinct repos (Epic Boundary Rule 1) — job runtime support vs. quota/admission configuration.

Note: E005 carries P1 despite HLR-4 being P2 — the `docs-authoring` priority exception derives priority from the strategy's frontmatter (`priority: Major` → P1).

## Health Warnings

1. **Missing strategy sections** (non-blocking): the strategy has no Impacted Teams table, no Dependencies table, no Given/When/Then acceptance criteria, and no Non-Functional Requirements. Teams were derived from architecture-context owning teams (RHOAI Serving for Serving Runtimes/KServe; Distributed Workloads for Training Operator/Distributed Workloads). Epic ACs were derived from HLR text.
2. **Hardware access (open question 1) is an availability precondition, not an epic or AC**: procurement / partner-lab access for dedicated AMD Instinct nodes is granted by parties outside the strategy. It is recorded as a Risk on E001; E001's ACs sit on the deliverable (the validated report and reproducible environment configuration), which the epic's work does produce. If access is not secured, the campaign — and therefore all downstream work — slips; this is a schedule risk, not a DAG edge.
3. **Upstream ROCm build cadence (open question 2)**: external dependency with uncertain timing, controlled by AMD and upstream communities. It does not change which epics exist — productization proceeds regardless and pins whatever ROCm image is released. Captured as a re-pinning AC on E002 plus a risk note; no DAG edge, no separate epic (no PR/RFC is submitted by us; Rule 21 precondition handling).
4. **KServe is a passive component**: the strategy lists KServe as affected, but no KServe code change is implied — vLLM runtimes execute under existing KServe InferenceServices/ServingRuntime lifecycle. Validation that InferenceServices deploy and serve with the ROCm runtime is folded in as an AC on E002 (nearest active component, same owning team), per the passive-component rule.
5. **Docs team assumption**: with no Impacted Teams table, E005 is assigned to RHOAI Serving (owner of the P0 serving scope and the validated model list). Confirm whether a documentation team should own it.
6. **AMD node enablement folded into E001**: no platform component in the strategy's affected list owns an AMD GPU device plugin/operator (the platform's accelerator discovery today is the NVIDIA GPU Operator). Standing up the validation environment (ROCm driver stack, device plugin exposing amd.com/gpu) is part of the campaign's scope. Conditional re-split trigger: if AMD GPU node enablement becomes a productized platform concern (an AMD GPU Operator equivalent under Platform Operator), split it out as a separate Implementation epic at that point.
